Very large scenes

Source: vignettes/articles/big-data.Rmd
big-data.Rmd

The default widget draws one SVG node per mark. That is what makes hover, per-element styling and screen-reader focus work, and it is fine up to a few thousand marks. It stops being fine well before you reach a scientific-scale scatter: 150,000 keyed points as per-element SVG come to roughly 75 MB and 150,000 DOM nodes. That is slow to build, slow to ship and slow to hover.

Above a threshold, the widget switches to raster mode. It keeps the plot’s chrome as SVG, draws the marks as an image, and then swaps in sharper and more interactive drawings of the marks as you zoom in. Everything on this page is automatic. Settings and fallbacks lists the settings, in render_options(), that change it.

Raster mode

Above raster_threshold keyed elements (default 20000), render_options(mode = "auto") (the default) leaves the per-element SVG behind:

library(vellumplot)

set.seed(1)
n <- 30000
big <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(n),
  y = rnorm(n),
  g = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), n, replace = TRUE),
  id = seq_len(n)
)
vplot(big) |>
  mark_point(x = x, y = y, color = g, data_id = id, size = 1) |>
  as_widget()

That scatter has 30,000 keyed points, so "auto" chose raster mode. What reaches the browser is:

  • The chrome as SVG. Axes, gridlines, titles, the legend and any text stay real SVG, exactly as in SVG mode. Furniture drawn after the marks in the plot (a mark_rule() or annotate() added after the points) goes in its own SVG layer on top of them.
  • The keyed marks as one PNG. vellum renders only the keyed marks onto a transparent image, at twice the plot’s pixel resolution, so it stays sharp on HiDPI screens. Each panel shows it inside its own clipped, zoomable group.
  • An element index. Keys, boxes and exact geometry for every mark, sent as compact columns. Hover, click, brush and lasso hit-test against it, so they work without any per-point DOM.
  • The display list. vellum’s marks-only display list: each keyed mark’s exact device-pixel geometry and paint (shape, fill, stroke, width, dash, alpha) in paint order. The zoomed-in tiers below draw from it.

Because the chrome is real SVG, zoom works as it does in SVG mode. The data region zooms and the axes re-tick for the visible range. Facet panels zoom together, each re-ticking its own axes, and the navigator, linked views and vellumplot::bind_scale() overview + detail all work on a raster plot.

Tiers as you zoom

The marks are drawn by one of three tiers, chosen when the view changes:

  1. Overview: the mark PNG. At the full view the browser shows vellum’s own anti-aliased image.

  2. Mid tier: exact redraw from the display list. Once you zoom in, scaling the PNG would blur it, so the widget redraws the marks in view from the display list: their own shapes, colours, strokes and alpha, in the order vellum painted them, through each panel’s zoom and clip. The redraw is exact, not a magnified image.

    A list of 50,000 marks or more is drawn with WebGL2, where the browser has it. A million points redraw in about 10 ms, so pan and zoom stay live. Smaller lists, and lists WebGL2 cannot draw (such as gradients, dashed strokes, grouped marks, masks or text, and very large paths), are drawn on a 2D canvas instead. On the canvas, a view with more than 50,000 marks redraws once the gesture settles, with the scaled image standing in until then.

  3. Detail tier: real SVG nodes. Zoom in until fewer than detail_marks marks (default 3000) are in view and, once the view settles, those marks are built as keyed SVG nodes in their panel. From there on the plot behaves like SVG mode: hover and selection style the marks themselves instead of drawing rings, and the marks are focusable from the keyboard. Panning rebuilds the nodes for the new view. Zooming back out past 1.5 times the threshold returns to the mid tier.

Glyph marks (points and text) keep their pixel size in every tier, as in SVG mode, so zooming spreads a dense cloud apart instead of enlarging it.

The mid and detail tiers both need the display list. Marks the list draws only approximately (masks, effects, patterns, text) still come out right: they arrive as small images of their own, cut in paint order, and the tiers place those where they belong.

Selections, conditions and filters

Everything the plot declares reaches the raster tiers. The widget keeps each mark’s state (selected, dimmed, recoloured, hidden, muted) per key and applies it in whichever tier is drawing:

  • vellumplot::condition() colours, opacities and dimming;
  • vellumplot::filter_by() and cross-filters, which leave filtered-out marks undrawn;
  • legend legend_click = "hide" and "mute";
  • crosstalk filter_* inputs and vw_filter().

Selected marks are drawn above the other marks of their layer. While any of this state is active, the drawn list replaces the mark PNG even at the full view, so nothing waits for a zoom. Click a swatch in this legend to hide a series, or click a point to grey out the groups it is not in (click empty space to clear):

vplot(big) |>
  mark_point(x = x, y = y, data_id = id, size = 1,
             color = condition("hi", g, "grey85")) |>
  select_point("hi", on = "click", fields = "g") |>
  as_widget(legend_click = "hide")

Exports from the toolbar (SVG, PNG and copy) redraw the list at export resolution with the same state, so a zoomed or filtered export matches the screen.

Settings and fallbacks

You can force the strategy instead of letting "auto" decide, and tune each tier, with render_options():

as_widget(p, render = render_options(mode = "svg"))    # always per-element SVG
as_widget(p, render = render_options(mode = "raster")) # always raster mode
as_widget(p, render = render_options(raster_threshold = 50000)) # move the switch

as_widget(p, render = render_options(max_marks = 5e6))  # ship a bigger display list
as_widget(p, render = render_options(detail_marks = 0)) # no SVG detail tier
as_widget(p, render = render_options(webgl = "never"))  # 2D canvas only
as_widget(p, render = render_options(max_zoom = 20))    # zoom in at most 20x
  • max_marks (default 2 million) caps the marks whose exact geometry ships. With the default precision = "compact" a scatter’s widget takes about 6 MB per million points and several seconds per million to build. Above the cap, the widget ships only a bounding-box index and says so with a message. Zoomed-in marks are then drawn as plain dots in each mark’s own colour and marker shape, and there is no detail tier. A plot that big usually reads better as density, with vellumplot::mark_datashade() or vellumplot::mark_hex().
  • detail_marks (default 3000) is the mark count below which the detail tier takes over. 0 turns it off.
  • webgl: "auto" (default) uses WebGL2 for lists of 50,000 marks or more; "always" uses it for any list and "never" keeps the 2D canvas. If the browser has no WebGL2, or drops the context, the canvas takes over.
  • precision: "compact" (default) quantises the list’s coordinates to within 0.005 px, which roughly halves them; "f32" ships 32-bit floats.
  • max_zoom (default 100) caps the zoom per axis, in SVG and raster mode alike. At 100x vellum’s coordinate grid is still within half a screen pixel, so marks stay on their gridlines; past it they drift. It takes 1 to 10000.

When a tier can’t run, you get:

When What you get
WebGL2 unavailable, lost, or the list holds what it can’t draw the 2D canvas mid tier
More marks than max_marks the mark PNG, plain dots on zoom, no detail tier; conditions, filters and legend hide/mute are not drawn; marks hidden by the legend, crosstalk or vw_filter() stop answering hover and clicks, but filter_by() leaves its marks pickable
A panel the axis zoom can’t follow (polar, theme_void() graphs) the whole scene zooms as one, like an image

Use mode = "svg" when you want per-element nodes at every zoom (for example, screen-reader traversal of every mark) on a plot near the threshold and can afford them. Use mode = "raster" to opt a smaller plot into raster mode, or raise raster_threshold to keep SVG mode for longer.

What makes it responsive

A few changes carry the load, and they apply whether the plot ends up as SVG or raster.

Columnar payload. The keyed-element metadata is serialised as one array per field (all the keys, then all the x-coordinates, and so on) instead of one JSON object per element. Columns with few distinct values ship each value once plus a small code per mark, row-number keys ship as differences, and the display list’s coordinates ship as packed integers. A whole 200,000-point keyed scatter widget, display list and mark image included, comes to about 1.1 MB and builds in a few seconds.

Spatial index. Nearest-mark hover and rectangular brush hit-test against a Flatbush R-tree rather than scanning every element. The nearest-mark scan runs on every pointer move, so replacing an O(n) scan with an O(log n) query is the change you feel most on a dense plot.

Exact picking on top of it. The R-tree indexes bounding boxes, which are the right shape for a rectangular brush and the wrong one for deciding what the cursor is pointing at: a rising line’s box is the whole rectangle its endpoints span. So the R-tree shortlists candidates, and those are ranked by distance to the mark’s real geometry. A box distance is never greater than the distance to the shape inside it, so nothing in range is missed. A round mark is measured to its disc rather than the square around it at no extra cost, and in raster mode lines and polygons take their shapes from the display list rather than a second copy.

Cheaper hover dim. Above a threshold, hovering dims the whole plot once through the container’s opacity and redraws just the hovered marks crisply in a small overlay, instead of restyling every element in CSS, which forced a full-scene style recalc on each hover. Small and moderate plots keep the exact per-mark dim.

Small and moderate plots never enter raster mode and behave exactly as on the interactive tour.
